mcqs.question: You're building a grammar-checking tool. Why might removing stopwords hurt this task?
options: Stopword removal is only defined for languages other than English
Stopwords always increase vocabulary size beyond what any model can handle
Stopwords like "is" and "not" carry the grammatical and negation signal the tool needs to catch
Removing stopwords makes tokenization fail on punctuation
mcqs.explanation: Stopword removal is task-dependent: for keyword search it cuts noise, but for grammar checking or translation, function words ("is", "not", "the") carry structural and negation meaning that the task needs. Option B misdescribes vocabulary growth (that's an n-gram/subword issue), C is false (stopword lists exist per-language, not "non-English only"), and D confuses stopword removal with tokenization, a separate pipeline step.

mcqs.question: In a corpus of 10,000 product reviews, why would TF-IDF assign a low score to the word "product" even if it appears many times in every review?
options: TF-IDF caps the maximum count any single word can contribute per document
TF-IDF ignores words that appear in the title of a review
TF-IDF only scores nouns, and "product" is misclassified as a stopword
"Product" appears in nearly every document, so its inverse-document-frequency term drives its weight down despite high local frequency
mcqs.explanation: TF-IDF multiplies local frequency (TF) by inverse document frequency (IDF), and a word appearing in almost every document gets an IDF near zero — that's the whole point of the metric, distinguishing globally common words from locally distinctive ones. The other options invent mechanisms TF-IDF doesn't have (no count cap, no POS filtering, no title-awareness).

mcqs.question: A sentiment classifier using unigram Bag-of-Words misclassifies "not good" as positive. Which change most directly addresses this specific failure?
options: Add bigrams to the vocabulary so "not good" is captured as one feature distinct from "good" alone
Switch from Bag-of-Words counts to raw TF-IDF weighting
Increase the size of the training set without changing the representation
Apply stemming to reduce "good" and "not" to a common root
mcqs.explanation: The failure is a representation problem: unigram BoW sees "not" and "good" as independent counts, losing the negation relationship entirely. Bigrams add "not_good" as its own feature, directly encoding the negation. TF-IDF re-weights unigram counts but doesn't add order information (still tempting since it sounds like an upgrade); more data doesn't fix a representation that structurally can't see word order; stemming operates on individual words and has no effect on this issue.

mcqs.question: A word-level tokenizer trained on English news text sees the informal word "gonna" for the first time at inference. What happens, and how would a BPE tokenizer differ?
options: Both tokenizers would fail identically, since neither can handle unseen words
The word-level tokenizer maps it to an out-of-vocabulary token, losing information; BPE decomposes it into known subword pieces, preserving partial signal
The word-level tokenizer automatically expands its vocabulary at inference time to include "gonna"
BPE would also emit an out-of-vocabulary token, since it only operates on whole words
mcqs.explanation: This is precisely the gap subword tokenization closes: word-level vocabularies are fixed and finite, so any unseen word becomes a single `<UNK>` token with no information; BPE/WordPiece can always fall back to smaller known pieces (or characters), so "gonna" might become "gon" + "na", preserving some signal. Vocabularies don't expand live at inference (C is wrong), and BPE's entire design point is operating below the word level (D is wrong).
